title: Magnetic field in a 2D section
subtitle: Flux, leakage and the iron path
intro: An advanced lab rather than a challenge. It assumes you already know what flux is, what a magnetic circuit is, and why iron carries one better than air. Carry a required flux through the core on an ampere-turn budget, and watch how much of it takes the air path instead.

challenge.statement: Size the cross-section to carry 4.5 mWb per metre of depth through the iron, using no more than 3600 ampere-turns in each side of the winding, and keeping less than 1 % of the flux out of the core. Runs that leave the model's domain of validity do not count.
challenge.next_step: the same flux through a different core geometry
challenge.plain_statement: Carry 4.5 mWb per metre of depth through the core on no more than 3600 A of ampere-turns, and keep the leakage under 1 %. The attempt only counts inside the model's stated limits.

prediction.question: Which change do you think costs the most flux?

explain.heading: The field prefers iron, but it has to cross the air
body: Iron offers the flux a far easier path than air. In the gap, though, the field has no alternative. A few millimetres of air can therefore dominate the behaviour of the whole circuit.
In your attempt the core carries {flux} mWb per metre of depth on {ampereTurns} ampere-turns: that number, not how good the iron is, decides whether the target is met.

explain.heading: Leakage is not a defect in the computation
body: Some of the flux closes through the air beside the core instead of through the gap. That is what the field does, not an error: the leakage number says how much of the winding's work is going somewhere the circuit was not designed to use.
In your attempt {leakage}% of the flux misses the core this way.

explain.heading: This core is linear, and a real one is not
body: The model uses a constant relative permeability for the material you select. A real soft steel saturates: past a certain field, more current buys much less flux. Nothing in this page will show you that, which is a limit of the model rather than a property of the iron.

teacher.objective: Read a magnetic circuit as a path with unequal reluctances, and locate where the field actually goes.
teacher.prediction: How much flux does one more millimetre of air cost?
teacher.misconception: Iron carries the field, so the air gap is a detail.
teacher.discussion: Why is iron essential and yet the air the thing that usually decides the result?
teacher.prerequisites: Magnetic flux, field, and the idea of a magnetic circuit.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.lead: Get 4.5 mWb per metre of depth up the core, on an ampere-turn budget, without leaking it.
body: The default cross-section carries about 3.45 mWb/m at 3000 ampere-turns and leaks 1.7 % of its flux past the iron, so it misses two of the three targets. The budget is what makes this a design problem rather than a dial: **3600 ampere-turns** is close to the most this window can usefully be given, so the extra flux has to come out of the magnetic circuit and not out of the current.

Three things are worth knowing before you start. **The flux is limited by the air, not by the iron** — at μᵣ = 1000 the core is already a thousand times the easier path, so making it better buys almost nothing while shortening the *return* buys a lot. **Ampere-turns are winding thickness times half-height times current density**, so the same budget can be spent as a thin tall coil or a fat short one, and those are not equivalent. And **leakage is set by the air gap**: widen it and a rapidly growing share of the flux misses the core entirely. How large a share is a question for the computation and for the geometry you have drawn, not for a table.

There is more than one cross-section that passes. Find one, keep the run, then find a different one that also passes and compare the two — the run table exists to make that comparison, not to store screenshots.

sections.heading: The model
body: Static, two-dimensional, linear magnetostatics for a current flowing perpendicular to the plane. With the current out of plane the magnetic vector potential has only that component, and the whole problem collapses to one scalar equation:
**−∇·( ν ∇A_z ) = J_z**, with **ν = 1/(μ₀ μᵣ)** the reluctivity, and **B = ( ∂A_z/∂y , −∂A_z/∂x )**.

That is worth reading twice, because two useful facts fall straight out of it. The contour lines of A_z **are** the magnetic field lines. And the flux crossing any curve, per metre of depth, is simply the difference in A_z between its two ends — which is why every flux on this page is a subtraction rather than an integral, and why it can be checked against one.
**Material.** Linear and isotropic: μᵣ is a constant you set, and the solver applies it whatever the field. Copper is non-magnetic and carries the current; air is μᵣ = 1 and carries none.

**No initial conditions.** The problem is static, so there is no state at *t* = 0. Where a transient exercise would list one, this page has nothing to list, and inventing something to fill the gap would be a lie about the model.
**Units.** SI throughout. The sliders are in millimetres and A/mm² because that is how a coil is thought about; everything is converted at the boundary, and every reported number is SI.

**Per metre of depth.** A two-dimensional slice has no length, so a flux here is a flux *per metre* (Wb/m) and an energy an energy per metre (J/m). Multiply by the real depth to get the three-dimensional quantity — and then read the limits, because a real magnet has ends and this one does not.

**The sign of the flux** is fixed by the winding sense, which this page fixes too: current out of the page on the right, into it on the left. The reported flux is negative because it crosses the mid-plane downward, and the headline tiles and the mission show its magnitude. The signed value stays in the full table and in the exported row, where a program reads it.

sections.heading: Boundary conditions
body: **On the outer edge of the window: A_z = 0**, on all four sides. Since field lines are contours of A_z, a constant value on the boundary means the boundary *is* a field line: the flux is made to close inside the modelled window rather than escaping to infinity.

That is a modelling choice and not a physical wall, so the window has to be comfortably larger than the magnet. This page sizes it automatically at **eight times the magnet's half-extent**, which holds the energy against the boundary below about half a per cent in every configuration the sliders can reach. It is checked on every run and reported under *How far to trust it*: past 1 % the run is disqualified, because at that point the box is setting the answer as much as the magnet is.

**At the iron/air interface: nothing is imposed.** The normal component of **B** and the tangential component of **H** are continuous there, and both follow from the equation rather than being applied to it. What the solver does have to get right is the *discretisation* of that interface, which is why the grid puts a cell face on every material boundary instead of rasterising it.

**On the windings: no condition either.** A winding is a region carrying a current density, not a boundary. The current is the only source in the whole problem — iron carrying no current makes no field on its own, and everything on the screen is the winding's field, redistributed by the iron.

sections.heading: Physical inputs
body: **Core half-width** thickens the iron path. It sets the area the flux has to fit through, so it controls the flux *density* more than the flux.

**Air gap** pushes the winding away from the core — the space insulation and formers take. It costs leakage: the further the copper is from the iron, the more of its field closes through air before reaching the core.

**Winding thickness** adds copper outward, and with it ampere-turns. The coil is measured outward from the core rather than from the axis, so no combination of sliders can be dragged into a geometry the solver would refuse.

**Half-height** lengthens the core and the coil along the axis. It buys ampere-turns *and* shortens the return path relative to the magnet, which is why it is usually the most effective slider on this page.

**Core permeability μᵣ** moves in decades, because that is how the quantity behaves: 1 means no core at all, and 10³–10⁴ is real soft iron or ferrite. Take it from 1000 to 10 000 and watch how little happens — three tenths of a per cent more flux for ten times the iron, because the flux still has to return through air and improving the easy half of a series path buys nothing.

**Current density** scales the source. Because the material is linear, doubling it doubles every field exactly and changes nothing about the shape of the solution. That is a property of the model rather than of iron, and it is the first limit below.

The **modelled window is not among these**, deliberately. It is derived from the magnet at a fixed ratio, because it is a numerical choice: it should not change the answer, and every run says how nearly that is true.

sections.heading: The fields
body: **|B|** is the flux density, in tesla — what a Hall probe or a Gauss meter reads. Look at the bright band inside the core, and how abruptly it ends at the surface of the iron.

**A_z** is the vector potential, and its contour lines **are** the magnetic field lines. Watch them run up the core and close their loops out through the air. The flux between any two adjacent lines is the same everywhere, so where the lines crowd, the field is strong — the whole picture in one image.

**H** is the field strength. Switch between it and |B| with the core at μᵣ = 1000: B is large in the iron and H is small there, and in the air it is the other way round. That contrast *is* what permeability means — the core carries flux at almost no cost in H.

**μᵣ** is not a result but a check on the model: it shows where the solver put the iron. Every material boundary lands on a cell face rather than being staircased onto a raster, which is what makes the core exactly as wide as it was drawn, at every resolution.
The solver also publishes **B as a vector**, so the workspace can draw glyphs and integrate streamlines rather than only colour a magnitude. Hover anywhere to read the value under the cursor.

sections.heading: The engineering answer
body: **Core flux Φ′**, per metre of depth, across the core's mid-plane — the horizontal line through the middle of the iron, where the flux in a solenoid is greatest and where a designer would put a search coil. It is the drop in A_z between the two edges of the core, and it is computed a second time by integrating **B** along the same line so the two can be compared.

**Mean flux density B̄** is that flux divided by the core's width, and **the worst section** is the same quantity evaluated at every height along the core and maximised. For a straight bar the two are nearly equal; for a stepped or tapered core they would not be, and it is the worst section that saturates first.

**Leakage** is the share of the flux crossing the mid-plane that misses the iron. The surface it is measured against is not a choice: it runs between the two points where the vertical component of **B** changes sign, which is where the flux going one way stops and the return begins. Ending the surface where the integrand vanishes is what makes the number insensitive to exactly where it is put.
**Ampere-turns** is the current through one side of the winding. It needs no solve at all — it is an integral over the geometry — and it is the budget the challenge is set against.

**Stored energy** is ½∫**B**·**H** over the window, and **permeance** is the core flux per ampere-turn: the magnetic circuit's own figure of merit. Multiply permeance by turns squared and by the real depth to get an inductance.

**There is no peak flux density here, and that is deliberate.** The corner of the core is a singularity of the exact solution: refine the mesh and the pointwise maximum keeps climbing — 0.148, 0.185, 0.230, 0.290 T for the same magnet at four resolutions — because there is nothing there to resolve. A number that grows every time you look harder is not a measurement, so this exercise reports section averages, which converge, and says so rather than printing the peak and hoping.

**There is no gap force either.** This cross-section has no working air gap: a straight bar core between two opposed windings is symmetric, so the net force on it is exactly zero and any number reported would be rounding error. A gap force needs a C-core and an armature — a different cross-section.

sections.heading: How the numbers are checked
body: **Energy balance.** The stored energy computed from the field, ½∫**B**·**H**, against the same energy computed from the sources, ½∫A_z J_z. They are equal for a linear material and they share the solution and nothing else, so the gap between them is the headline residual — it catches both a solve that stopped early and a mesh too coarse to carry the field.
**The core flux, two ways.** Once as the drop in A_z across the core, once by integrating **B** along the same line. Same surface, two independent routes.

**Ampère's law.** The circulation of **H** around a contour enclosing one winding, against the current that contour encloses. It runs along cell centres through the air rather than along cell faces, deliberately: on faces the finite-volume equations telescope and the identity would hold to the solver's tolerance and tell you nothing, so it is placed where it measures the reconstructed field instead. Switch its annotation layer on to see exactly where it runs.

**Refinement.** The same problem solved again at twice the resolution, reporting how far the mean flux density moved. It is the only check that measures the *mesh*, it costs four times the cells, and when it is turned off the page says the check was not run rather than showing a zero.

**The linear residual.** How far the conjugate-gradient solve actually got, against the tolerance it was asked for. Worth having on the screen, because the alternative is the failure this exercise was built to avoid: a solver that takes a fixed number of sweeps, stops, and returns something that looks exactly like a converged answer.

sections.heading: Limits of the model
body: The material is **linear**: μᵣ is a constant you set, and the solver applies it whatever the field. Real iron **saturates** — above roughly 1.5 T for common steels its permeability collapses towards that of air, and no amount of extra current buys much more flux. Every run checks the busiest section of the core against that threshold and disqualifies itself above it. Note which way the error runs: past saturation this model **overestimates**, because it keeps returning flux in proportion to current and a real core does not.
There is no **hysteresis** and no remanence: turn the current off in this model and the field is exactly zero, which is not what happens to a real iron core.

This is a **two-dimensional cross-section**, which means an infinitely long magnet. A real solenoid has ends, and at those ends the flux fringes outward in a way no 2-D slice can show. Treat the picture as the middle of something long, and every flux as a flux per metre of that length.

The outer boundary imposes **A_z = 0**, which confines the flux to the modelled window. The real field extends indefinitely, weakening with distance; here it is made to close inside the box. The window is sized at eight times the magnet for that reason, and the share of the stored energy lying against the boundary is reported on every run.
Everything is **static**. No eddy currents, no skin effect, no inductive transient — this is the field once the current has settled, not the field while it is changing.
The winding is a **uniform block of current density**, not individual turns. The ampere-turns are right and the fine structure between conductors is absent.

The **corners of the core are singular**, and that is a property of the exact solution rather than of the mesh. It is why no pointwise peak field is reported, and why every number that *is* reported is an integral — a flux, a section average, an energy — which a singularity carries no weight in.
The result is not a magnetic design and must not be used to size anything.
